bib.title: Code as Policies: Language Model Programs for Embodied Control

question: Can code-writing LLMs, prompted few-shot, write robot policy code that processes perception outputs and parameterizes control primitives, without any training?
hypothesis: Code-writing LLMs can be re-purposed to write robot policy code from natural language commands via few-shot prompting, generalizing to new instructions.
contributions: code as policies: a formulation of using LLMs to write robot code
a method for hierarchical code-gen that improves state-of-the-art on both robotics and standard code-gen problems with 39.8% P@1 on HumanEval
a new benchmark (RoboCodeGen) to evaluate future language models on robotics code-gen problems
ablations that analyze how CaP improves metrics of generalization and that it abides by scaling laws

method.summary: Few-shot prompt a code-completion LLM with Hints (imports) and Examples (comment-to-code pairs) so it writes Python language model programs (LMPs) that call perception and control APIs. Undefined functions in generated code are found by AST parsing and filled by a function-generating LMP, depth-first. Code is checked (no imports, no __ names, no exec/eval) then run with exec.
method.task: language-instructed robot policy code generation; code generation benchmarks

datasets.name: RoboCodeGen
datasets.source: introduced by this paper; human-written unit tests

datasets.name: Reasoning with code vs language benchmark
Simulated tabletop manipulation
datasets.size: 8 inherited long-horizon tasks + 6 new spatial-geometric tasks; 10 colored blocks and 10 colored bowls; 50 trials per task
datasets.source: environment from Zeng et al. 2022 and Huang et al. 2022

other.note: Codex sizes not public; used for all experiments unless stated

models.name: NL Planner
models.architecture: few-shot prompted LLM planner using natural language instead of code

other.use: off-the-shelf open-vocab detector, tabletop and whiteboard

inference.decoding: greedy (temperature 0) for all LMP experiments; HumanEval also sampled
inference.samples: HumanEval P@1, P@10, P@100 from N samples at temperature 0.8; LMPs always one greedy output; number of repeated runs of RoboCodeGen not stated
inference.prompting: few-shot: Hints (import statements) plus Examples (comment instruction followed by code); HumanEval prompts contain only 2 examples; sim tabletop: one example rollout per task; session kept by appending instructions and responses

parameters.safety_check: no import statements, no variables beginning with __, no exec or eval calls
parameters.hierarchical_gen: parse AST, find undefined functions, call function-generating LMP, recurse depth-first
parameters.position_correct: all coordinates within 1cm of ground truth

metrics.name: pass rate
metrics.definition: percentage of generated code passing human-written unit tests

metrics.name: P@N (HumanEval)
metrics.definition: correctness across N samples decoded at temperature 0.8

metrics.name: task success rate
metrics.definition: success over 50 trials per task with sampled attributes and scenes

baselines: code-davinci-001 and PaLM Coder (from Chowdhery et al. 2022)
eval.protocol: Sim tabletop: 50 trials per task, seen/unseen split of instructions and attributes; real-robot domains are qualitative demos with no quantitative evaluation.

limits: Restricted by what perception APIs can describe and which control primitives exist; only a handful of named primitive parameters can be adjusted without oversaturating prompts.
Struggles with significantly longer or more complex commands, or commands at a different abstraction level than the Examples (e.g. build a house with blocks).
Assumes all instructions are feasible; cannot tell whether a response will be correct a priori.
Quantitative evaluation limited to constrained simulated tasks; real-robot domains have no quantitative evaluation.
Cross-embodiment ability is brittle; reactive controllers are simple and no gain tuning from execution feedback.
Sampling many solutions (P@100) is impractical for LMPs, so only greedy output is used.
Codex model sizes not public; code-davinci-002 compared with code-davinci-001 in prior works.
